vignette: Marcus was twelve when the basement light flickered and died, leaving only the damp cold of the concrete floor seeping through the thin cotton of his shirt. He remembered the specific, scratchy weave of the heavy wool blanket his stepfather used to pin his arms, the way the rough fibers bit into his forearms. Before that, there had always been the sound of heavy boots crossing the hardwood above, a rhythmic thud that grew closer, more deliberate, until the doorknob turned. The cold would follow first, a sharp bite against his skin when the door opened, and then the pressure. Marcus had come to believe that safety was a story other people told themselves. Even now, years later, he found it impossible to believe the words of a friend who told him he was safe, or a mechanic who assured him the brakes on his sedan were fine. His body kept reacting as if he were still pinned in that dark room, muscles locking, breath shortening, as though the cold and the weight were never truly gone. Over time, the world outside the house became a series of narrow streets where the old patterns waited. He started driving a taxi in his early twenties, navigating the grid of his city with his eyes constantly scanning the rearview mirror and the periphery of the rear window. What frightened him most was the tactile shift of a passenger's winter coat brushing the vinyl seat, or the sudden draft from a cracked window that sent a familiar chill across his neck. He would catch himself flinching at the sound of hurried footsteps on the sidewalk behind his parked cab, his hands gripping the steering wheel until his knuckles ached. He was certain that if he stopped moving, if he let himself settle into stillness, the boots would return. The alertness never left him, and he found himself taking extra shifts to keep his hands busy, sometimes taking too many risks on slick roads just to feel a rush that drowned out the waiting dread. His body felt like a traitor, constantly sounding alarms in the absence of real threats. He had come to believe he was permanently changed for the worse, wired to anticipate violence rather than peace. The habits formed quietly. He stopped answering calls from his childhood church group and stopped visiting the barbershop where he had once gone to cut his hair, telling himself it was just a busy season, though he knew he had lost his connection to the people who used to know him. When his phone buzzed with messages from women who asked to meet, he would silence it, pulling his phone up to scroll through random posts or turning the radio up until it filled the cabin, distracting himself while navigating toward empty neighborhoods where he could avoid dropping passengers who tried to make conversation. He began to take drugs to sleep, the chemical fog at least muting the edge of his nerves, though it left him sluggish behind the wheel. The consequences accumulated in the empty passenger seat and the mounting balance on his credit card, but the most tangible shift was in how he moved through his own days, treating every interaction as a potential breach of perimeter. It was the night he nearly drifted into oncoming traffic after a passenger complained about the temperature, his hand twitching toward the glove compartment where he kept the drugs, that he finally turned the engine off and walked to the clinic across the street. He stood outside the sliding doors, watching his breath fog in the air, terrified that he was already too broken to ever sit still without counting exits, but desperate enough to hope that someone might help him untangle the cold, the rough wool, and the footsteps so he could finally drive without looking over his shoulder.
